Area.evidence_source: The participants seldom disclosed their mental illness to others for fear of being ridiculed. They characterized their identity as mentally ill patients, and tended to accept that they had limited opportunities in life, such as finding a mate for marriage or securing a job. A male participant in his late 20s poignantly talked about how he viewed himself since he became mentally ill at age 16: "I have not wanted to live since I became ill. I don't like myself… My mind is not sharp. I am not normal… In my next life, I want to be a real person: very disciplined, smart, does a good job at work." A young female participant talked about her perception of others since she became mentally ill: "People don't want to mingle with you when they know you have a mental illness; they look at you differently." A retired female participant discussed her fear of other people finding out about her mental illness when she was working: "They would take advantage of me or look down at me if they knew." A middle-aged male participant described the changes in his lifestyle: "Before I became ill, I used to go out without any hesitations. Now, I hardly take walks or go to the park because I have to think over and over again whether my behavior is normal or not when I meet other people."
